newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: THIS BUD'S FOR YOU, BUT WHOSE BUD IS IT?.
newsitem.headline: THIS BUD'S FOR YOU, BUT WHOSE BUD IS IT?.

text.p: Czech Budejovicky Budvar n.p. said on Wednesday it will soon brew and export a powerful version of its lager to be called "Bud", firing another shot in the tiny brewery's battle with U.S. Anheuser Busch.

In a move which may irk makers of the U.S. Budweiser, the brewer in the southern Czech city of Budejovice (Budweis in German) said it would export "Bud" with 7.2 percent alcohol, to countries where it holds rights to the "Budweiser" trademark.
"We want to export this beer to all the markets where we have a registered trade mark," Ales Kocvera, Budvar's public relations director told Reuters.
Under a 1911 agreement, Budvar owns exclusive rights to "Budweiser" and derivations of the name in much of Europe.

Czechs consider the seven centuries of Budweis brewing tradition to be part of their national heritage, and say Busch's version of Budweiser, which German immigrants to the United States began brewing last century, is a weak immitation.
Busch, the world's largest brewer, has sold its Budweiser under "Bud" in some markets in Europe, while keeping a lock on the trademark in America and much of the rest of the world.
In Germany, Busch is marketing Budweiser simply as "B" beer.

Kocvera added that Budvar was still seeking legal advice about selling under the Bud name in Germany where Bitburger beer is sold under the name "Bit", which some lawyers have argued may be considered too close to "Bud".
A similar situation, he said, applied in Britain.
Budvar said that its new beer would be produced initially in small quantities.
"I think that if we sold 5,000 to 10,000 hectolitres of this product this year it would be a success," said Kocvera.

Anheuser Busch and the Czech government broke off talks last year over a selling minority stake in the state-owned Budvar to the American company as part of a comprehensive settlement of the trademark dispute and the Czech brewery's privatistaion.
After talks broke down both companies have been poised to fight for their turf and are currently in litigation over use of the name in Finland.

The Czech government is considering a management buyout of Budvar and the Agriculture Ministry said in January that the much-delayed privatisation of Budvar should go ahead regardless of the continuing trademark dispute with Anheuser.
